concepts.definition: A consistent logical table state selected by committed metadata at a particular version.
concepts.example: Version v0 selects A0 and C, so it contains 18 inspected units.

concepts.definition: New data prepared by a writer before its changes become a committed table version.
concepts.example: A1 can exist while the current snapshot still contains A0 and C.

concepts.definition: A successful transaction boundary that makes a new table state visible.
concepts.example: v1 removes A0 from the current selection, adds A1 and retains C.

concepts.definition: Reading a retained earlier table version under the environment’s supported retention and runtime rules.
concepts.example: Reconstructing v0 needs its history and the A0 and C data files.

concepts.definition: Agreement between published data and the defined business identity, ordering and metric rules.
concepts.example: A transaction can atomically commit both A revisions even though only the latest should count.

concepts.definition: Checking a write against the table’s expected structural types and fields.
concepts.example: An integer -3 can fit an integer column while violating a nonnegative inspection rule.

concepts.definition: The compatibility requirements a client must satisfy to read or write the table’s enabled features.
concepts.example: A feature-enabled table may remain valid while an older external reader can no longer interpret it.

concepts.definition: Preparing work and checking for conflicting committed changes before accepting the new transaction.
concepts.example: Two writers both replacing A0 cannot independently assume their original read is still current.

concepts.definition: Comparing a result with the expected population and quantities under a stated contract.
concepts.example: If C changes from 8 to 6 after A is already 12, the new total is 18.

concepts.definition: Metadata identifying rows in a data file that are logically removed from the current table state.
concepts.example: A file holds rows A and C, but a deletion vector excludes A from the current logical read.

concepts.definition: A table feature separating logical column identities/names from their physical representation in data files.
concepts.example: A logical field can be renamed from checked_units to inspected_units without rewriting its existing data values.

concepts.definition: A table interface exposing row changes and change metadata between committed table versions.
concepts.example: An update from inspected=12 to inspected=14 can expose before and after images for the same business row.

beats.title: The folder is not the table
beats.outcome: Select the files belonging to one committed snapshot.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-delta-folder-concept|snapshot]] says which stored data belongs to one table version. Here the folder contains A0, A1 and C, but version v0 selects only A0 and C. Add the selected quantities: 10 + 8 = 18 inspected units. File existence and table membership answer different questions.

samajh.text: Godown mein saara samaan pada ho sakta hai, par current stock ka hisaab register se milta hai. Sirf shelves ginoge toh replaced maal bhi count ho jayega. Yahan files shelves jaisi hain; snapshot batata hai kaunsi files is version ka part hain.
samajh.mapping: Shelves represent physical files; the register represents membership.
samajh.boundary: The analogy explains membership, not the transaction protocol.

handbook.markdown:
The reader needs a table state, not a recursive sum of the directory. Our deliberately small example treats each file as one inspection contribution; actual files usually contain many rows. A0 and A1 are alternative representations of inspection A. C is unchanged. Selecting both A files would count two representations of the same contribution.

Trace the calculation in two steps: first resolve membership for v0; then evaluate the query over that membership. The membership is {A0, C}; the aggregate is 18. A different query might count rows or filter a plant, but it must still begin from the same consistent snapshot. Filename age is not the selection rule.

Storage holds bytes, compute performs the calculation, Delta supplies the table-state protocol, and governance controls permitted access. Those responsibilities work together; a transaction log does not grant a user permission or run their query. Avoid reading Delta directories as uncoordinated Parquet files when you intend Delta table semantics. This visual is an authored model, not an executed Delta transaction.

beats.recap: A snapshot chooses membership before a query calculates a total.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: Writing a file is not committing
beats.outcome: Predict a failure before commit without promoting staged data.
beats.explanation: The writer prepares A1 with a corrected value of 12. A [[dbxfe-delta-stage-concept|staged write]] is not yet the current table. Until validation and commit succeed, a current reader still selects A0 and C and obtains 18. Move the visual to the failed-writer state: the file can remain present without entering the snapshot.

samajh.text: Corrected bill draft ho gaya, lekin approve nahi hua. Draft ka number dekh kar final accounts badal doge toh galat hoga. A1 ready hai; commit ke baad hi woh current table ka part ban sakti hai. Failure se draft file reh sakti hai.
samajh.mapping: A prepared draft corresponds to staged data; approval corresponds to visibility after commit.
samajh.boundary: Delta uses a formal commit protocol, not manual invoice approval.

handbook.markdown:
A write has a preparation phase and a visibility boundary. In the classic file-replacement explanation, the writer reads the relevant prior state, writes candidate files, then validates whether its proposed change can commit. The preparation may take time and may fail. Readers do not infer success from the presence of those files.

Consider three observations: A1 exists, the writer process stopped, and the latest committed table version remains v0. Only the third observation establishes the reader state in this example. A file timestamp cannot replace transaction evidence. Conversely, a client losing its response is not proof that the commit failed; inspect committed state before retrying an ambiguous operation.

For this beat the failure point is explicitly before commit, so 18 is unambiguous. Later recovery lessons examine failures after publication, where the answer differs. Do not delete arbitrary files to repair this demonstration in a real environment. Cleanup and retention follow table-management rules. The protected boundary is table visibility, not every external side effect a writer might also perform.

beats.recap: Prepared bytes are not evidence of a committed table change.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: The commit changes the picture
beats.outcome: Apply one atomic membership change and exclude the replaced file.
beats.explanation: A successful [[dbxfe-delta-commit-concept|commit]] changes the selection together: exclude A0, include A1, keep C. The new snapshot contains 12 + 8 = 20 inspected units. A0 may still physically exist. Logical removal from the current state is different from immediate deletion of its bytes; counting both versions would produce the wrong 30.

samajh.text: Purani 10 wali invoice ki jagah corrected 12 wali current hui. Dono invoices jod doge toh 10 extra count hoga. Old copy rakhna useful ho sakta hai, par current hisaab mein usko phir se include nahi karte. C ka 8 bilkul unchanged hai.
samajh.mapping: Replacement changes the current contribution while preserving the unchanged contribution.
samajh.boundary: Not every Delta update physically rewrites whole files this way.

handbook.markdown:
The important unit is the complete committed state transition. In our synthetic replacement, remove A0 and add A1 belong to the same change. A reader should not construct an invented intermediate state containing neither A file or both replacement files. An already-running read can retain a consistent earlier snapshot; a later read can select the newly committed version.

The arithmetic changes by +2 because 12 replaces 10. It does not change by +12. Keeping the unchanged C=8 visible helps separate replacement from addition. A1 does not mean a new independent inspection; the business contract says it is a corrected representation of A. That meaning is an input to the write, not a fact Delta invents.

Table version v1 is the transaction history position for the whole table. The source revision of A is a business ordering field. One transaction may contain many business revisions, and a maintenance transaction need not correspond to a new inspection revision. Diagnose a wrong total at both levels: did the writer choose the right rows, and did the table publish the intended change?

beats.recap: The new total is 20 because 12 replaces 10; it is not an extra 12.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: History needs the evidence to remain
beats.outcome: Identify why a historical read can fail despite a visible history entry.
beats.explanation: To reconstruct v0, [[dbxfe-delta-history-concept|time travel]] needs its history and required data files. A visible history entry is not enough if A0 has been removed. Retention and runtime limits also apply. The visual keeps the requested version fixed while removing one dependency: the result becomes unavailable, not an invented partial total.

samajh.text: Purani recipe mil gayi, par zaroori ingredients ab hain hi nahi. Recipe se pata hai kya chahiye tha; usse missing ingredient wapas nahi aa jata. Waise hi log old version ka selection batata hai, lekin required data files bhi bachni chahiye.
samajh.mapping: Recipe records requirements; ingredients represent retained data dependencies.
samajh.boundary: Runtime and retention checks add limits beyond this dependency analogy.

handbook.markdown:
Keep three questions separate: can you inspect operation history, are the necessary data files retained, and does the target runtime permit the requested age? They are related but not identical. A historical report should record the requested table version and the assumptions needed to reproduce it. A result silently missing A0 is not a successful reproduction of our v0.

The current AWS documentation describes separate history and deleted-file retention settings and runtime-specific time-travel age restrictions. Check the actual table and runtime; do not convert a remembered default into an archival promise. Increasing a setting later cannot resurrect bytes already deleted. Retention decisions also change storage obligations and costs.

A historical SELECT reads an old state; RESTORE changes current table state through a new operation. Downstream streaming consumers may treat restored data as new updates. That makes restore a coordinated recovery decision with reconciliation, not a harmless way to look backward. This lesson performs neither VACUUM nor RESTORE. Use a separate backup and recovery design when long-term archival or disaster recovery is required.

beats.recap: History plus required data plus supported runtime rules determine recoverability.

beats.title: A correct transaction can contain a wrong answer
beats.outcome: Separate table atomicity, source order and metric meaning.
beats.explanation: Atomic table behavior cannot decide whether A1 replaces A0 or represents a separate event. That is [[dbxfe-delta-meaning-concept|business correctness]]. If a writer submits the wrong business population, a successful transaction can preserve the mistake consistently. Keep source revision, table version and the metric definition separate when explaining what a commit proves.

handbook.markdown:
Start a correctness discussion by naming the grain: one current accepted inspection per inspection ID. Under that contract, an older representation of A cannot contribute alongside its replacement. If the source instead represented additive events, the rule would differ. The table format does not know which business contract the customer intended.

Use a small reconciliation ledger before blaming storage. Raw evidence may contain repeated deliveries, older revisions and invalid records. The resolver identifies the intended current population. A subsequent table transaction makes the selected update visible. Finally, the metric uses its agreed numerator and denominator. Failures at any layer can produce a plausible number.

For Cinderline, A2 has 12 inspected and 1 defective; C1 has 8 and 0. Accepted totals are 20 and 1, hence 5%. A successful commit containing 30 inspected units should be investigated as a population error, even if the log is internally consistent. Preserve the wrong run as diagnostic evidence rather than describing ACID as broken. The ingestion module teaches the corrected conservative publication gate explicitly.

beats.recap: Transactions protect a boundary; business rules define what should cross it.

beats.title: A type check is one part of a contract
beats.outcome: Distinguish structural schema checks from domain and cross-record checks.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-delta-schema-concept|schema enforcement]] checks structural compatibility. It does not make every accepted integer meaningful. A quantity of -3 may fit an integer column but violate our nonnegative rule; two individually valid records may still conflict about the same revision. Teach each check at the layer where it has the needed evidence.

handbook.markdown:
A schema makes a useful promise about representation: column names, data types and relevant nullability. Domain rules make a different promise, such as inspected being nonnegative and defective not exceeding inspected. Cross-record rules need relationships: one event ID should not describe two payloads under our source contract. Do not collapse these into a single green quality icon.

For the row A2=(12, 1), structural and quantity checks pass. For B1=(-3, 1), the numeric representation can still be well-formed, but the domain check fails. For two A2 rows with quantities 12 and 13, each can be structurally valid; their disagreement requires retained evidence. The resolution policy then determines whether publication can proceed.

Schema evolution is a deliberate change in the representation contract, not a cure for invalid data. Before allowing a new field or changed type, ask how existing producers, readers and transformations behave. A tolerant cast may convert a bad string into NULL, moving the failure into a later stage. Preserve that distinction and reconcile counts so a structurally convenient conversion does not silently change the metric population.

beats.recap: Structure, domain validity and identity agreement require different evidence.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: Can every client understand this table?
beats.outcome: Plan a feature change around all readers and writers.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-delta-protocol-concept|table protocol]] tells clients which capabilities they need. Enabling a feature can change that requirement even when familiar columns remain. Check the scheduled writer, SQL readers and external consumers before the change. “Our notebook works” tests one client; it does not prove the whole dependency graph still works.

handbook.markdown:
Make a dependency inventory with client, version, read/write role, feature support, owner and rollback plan. The table can remain internally valid while a client rejects a requirement it does not understand. Reader and writer requirements are related but distinct; checking one role cannot stand in for the other.

In the visual, a nightly writer, an analyst query and an external export all touch the same table. A notebook-only test misses the export. A bounded evaluation should include representative reads and writes on a nonproduction copy, followed by row-level reconciliation. Record which feature was enabled and which exact client versions were tested. Do not infer compatibility from a product logo.

Some features alter protocol requirements; not every feature can simply be turned off as a rollback. The current feature-compatibility page is the decision reference for the precise table and runtime. A schema-compatible projection does not necessarily remove an underlying protocol requirement. This module teaches how to frame the review; it does not authorize or execute a production feature upgrade.

beats.recap: A table feature change is also a change for its dependent clients.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: Validate before accepting a second writer
beats.outcome: Explain conflict detection without claiming all writes conflict.
beats.explanation: With [[dbxfe-delta-concurrent-concept|optimistic concurrency]], two writers can prepare work from the same starting state. Acceptance depends on what changed before each commit. An overlapping replacement may fail validation instead of silently corrupting state. Ordinary append pairs have different conflict behavior; “concurrent” alone does not tell you whether a particular pair will succeed.

handbook.markdown:
A useful explanation of optimistic concurrency separates preparation from acceptance. Both writers can do work, but the later committer must validate whether intervening changes invalidate what it assumed. If the conflict matters, a failure protects the table rather than indicating that partial changes should be counted.

Our writers both replace a file they read. This deliberately creates overlapping responsibility. A fresh retry must re-evaluate the latest table and the business ordering rule; blindly resubmitting stale conclusions can still be logically wrong. In contrast, ordinary independent append operations occupy a different cell in the documented conflict matrix. Do not say that every simultaneous write conflicts, or that every append succeeds regardless of other changes.

Metadata, schema and protocol changes can introduce additional conflicts. The physical scope read by a command also matters: apparently disjoint business predicates do not prove disjoint file access. Modern features may change detailed concurrency behavior. Use the current target-specific documentation when designing an actual workload. The visual is a reasoning exercise with an explicit classic replacement assumption, not a benchmark or executable concurrency test.

beats.recap: Concurrency is validated against actual overlapping changes and feature context.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: Predict the changed file set
beats.outcome: Transfer snapshot reasoning to a different corrected contribution.
beats.explanation: Now change C rather than A. Current v1 contains A1=12 and C0=8. A writer stages C1=6. Before commit the total stays 20; after a successful replacement it becomes 18. Use [[dbxfe-delta-transfer-concept|reconciliation]] to check both membership and arithmetic, then state what would be needed to reproduce the earlier 20.

handbook.markdown:
Write the selected set before calculating: v1={A1, C0}; v2={A1, C1}. The proposed correction reduces the accepted inspected population by 2. If your answer is 26, you counted both C representations. If your answer is 6, you dropped the unchanged A contribution. If your answer changes before commit, you confused staging with visibility.

Next separate observation from inference. Seeing C1 in storage proves preparation occurred, not acceptance. Seeing a committed v2 identifies the new table state, but business reconciliation must still confirm that C1 was the intended correction. Reproducing v1 later needs the actual old files and metadata, not just a remembered total.

For a customer explanation: “We can read a consistent committed table state and track its changes. We must separately validate your correction rule and retention needs.” This is stronger than promising that transactions make all data correct forever. Review the linked canonical cards on file membership, source versus table version and compatibility, then compare your applied answer with the model. Opening this recap is not evidence that you completed the exercise.

beats.recap: Select membership, apply the commit boundary, reconcile the quantity, then check historical dependencies.

extensionCards.prompt: Does a logically deleted row always disappear immediately from its Parquet file?
extensionCards.answer: No. With a deletion vector, readers exclude the row using metadata even while its bytes remain in the file.
extensionCards.explanation: The core visual selects whole files to explain snapshots. A [[dbxfe-delta-extension-deletion-vector-concept|deletion vector]] adds row-level interpretation: imagine file F contains A and C, and table metadata marks A deleted. A compatible table reader returns C; directly reading F as ordinary Parquet can still encounter A. Logical deletion, file rewrite and eventual removal of old files are different steps. The reviewed documentation describes separate operations for physically applying changes and cleaning old files. This card performs none of them and makes no erasure guarantee. Before enabling the feature, check every reader/writer’s compatibility and the particular operation being used.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Extends the simple file-selection model and prevents treating logical deletion as physical data erasure.

extensionCards.prompt: A change feed shows A=12 as update_preimage and A=14 as update_postimage. Should a current-state consumer sum them to 26?
extensionCards.answer: No. They describe the before and after images of one update; the intended current quantity is 14.
extensionCards.explanation: A [[dbxfe-delta-extension-change-images-concept|change data feed]] reports changes, not a bag of new independent business entities. The change-type label tells the consumer how to interpret each record. In this invented update, 12 is the prior quantity and 14 its replacement. A current-state sink should apply the update under its identity/order contract rather than append both into the current metric. The feed’s commit version identifies the table change and is not automatically the upstream inspection revision. Current Databricks documentation distinguishes automatic and legacy feed modes with different prerequisites. Select and verify that mode, starting boundary, schema behavior and retention before implementing a consumer.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Prevents double counting before/after images while connecting table changes to the upstream business contract.

extensionCards.prompt: Why can a metadata-only column rename still break a downstream consumer?
extensionCards.answer: The stored values may not need rewriting, but consumers can depend on the old logical name or unsupported schema-change behavior.
extensionCards.explanation: [[dbxfe-delta-extension-column-mapping-concept|column mapping]] allows supported logical renames and drops without rewriting every data file. Suppose a report expects checked_units and the table renames it inspected_units. The values can stay in existing files while the report’s reference becomes invalid. This is a contract change for consumers even if the storage operation is lightweight. Streaming reads, change feeds and clients that interpret physical directory names have documented compatibility constraints. Inventory those dependencies, test the intended rename with representative readers, and plan the schema transition. Metadata-only describes how data files are changed; it does not mean application behavior is unchanged.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Makes schema evolution a consumer-contract decision instead of equating low rewrite cost with low risk.

extensionCards.prompt: Does a Delta transaction-log checkpoint mean the same thing as a streaming-query checkpoint?
extensionCards.answer: No. A table-log checkpoint compacts table metadata state; a streaming checkpoint tracks a particular query’s progress and state.
extensionCards.explanation: The table-history documentation describes aggregated metadata checkpoints that avoid replaying all JSON history. That mechanism is distinct from the per-query recovery state taught in orchestration. Neither name alone promises archived data remains available.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A shared word should not lead to deleting the wrong recovery evidence.

recap.title: One table, four boundaries
recap.markdown:
**Files → selected snapshot → successful commit → retained historical dependencies.** Compute calculates; business rules select the intended population; compatibility determines which clients can interpret it. Review the canonical cards, or choose the researched extension cards deliberately.

**Next learning action:** continue with B2 Delta writes, evolution and table maintenance (`#/module/dbxfe-delta-writes`), which applies this snapshot model to MERGE, schema evolution and retention decisions.

appliedTask.title: Explain a failed correction
appliedTask.prompt: A1=12 and C0=8 are current. C1=6 is staged, then the writer fails before commit. Later a successful retry replaces C0. Give both totals and explain whether a visible v1 history entry is enough after C0 is deleted.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: The failed attempt leaves 20. The successful replacement yields 18. A visible v1 history entry is insufficient after required C0 is deleted; complete time travel also needs retained data and supported runtime/retention conditions.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer follows membership and the commit boundary, then checks historical dependencies. It does not infer acceptance from a file timestamp.
